# A. Warm-Up {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

`error × KP` for the **third time**. Today it steers the **eye**. 🛣️

## Where we left off

| You own | Built on |
|---|---|
| 📦 **`movements.py` begins** | `drive_straight` · `turn` |
| 📈 **`error × KP`** | the turn · the straight |
| 🛑 **D, damping** | brakes before overshoot |

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note}
## One thing up front
A script is **blind**. Today: **see → decide → steer.** Brightness only, colour names are a preview; colour-based missions are an optional extension.
:::
:::

⏱️ **Time: 5 minutes, then a bug hunt**

::: {.notes}
Anchor today in what they already own, or it feels like a brand-new mountain (it isn't — the plan flags the line day as the longest precisely because the *old* material was video-paced; live, it's one formula applied a third time). Recap `error × KP` from the gyro out loud. Today the robot opens its eyes — three new powers land: the color eye (reflection = the echo of its own light), the per-surface threshold, and `elif` (D5's `if`, now with more than two roads). Flag the reflection-vs-color point early and firmly — kids will want to "detect the green line"; stop that now, it's reflection for navigation; the red beeper is only a small colour preview. The day is eye → threshold → `if` → bang-bang → P on the line, then junction squaring — **the P follower + squaring pair is the gate** (it's what the anchor run actually uses); the PD upgrade is the stretch for squads that tune P early. If the cohort is still behind on programming, the afternoon flexes to library-consolidation practice instead of pushing PD. Keep this slide to five minutes: per the W2 delivery rhythm (decision #22), robots are out by minute 15.
:::

## 🔎 Bug hunt: the tune that didn't stick

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1-2|4-5"}
def make_it_sharper():
    KP = 12          # crank steering for the whole library… right?

make_it_sharper()
drive_straight(300)  # …still lazy. Nothing changed. 😤
```

::: {.qbox}
[Watch it stay lazy, then find the bug. Where *should* `KP = 12` live?]{.qtitle}
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
Inside a `def` you made a **local**, and it died the moment the function returned. **Change globals only at the top.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the course's one home for globals/shadowing (decision #65; delivered as a live hunt per decision #22), with the rescue on the next slide. Run the planted bug on the coach robot and let squads diagnose for ~5 minutes before any reveal; the 😤 must be theirs. Two live moments: (1) the fix — move `KP = 12` to the constants block, rerun, the straight sharpens; (2) `print(error)` after a run → NameError, proof that locals evaporate (and that's a *feature*: every verb gets private scratch names). Do NOT teach the `global` keyword — the constants-block discipline is strictly better. Coach's radar for W2–3: "I tuned it and it didn't stick" → first question is *where did you assign it?*
:::

## Two homes for a name 🗺️ {.smaller}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1-3|5-7"}
# Top of movements.py (GLOBAL)
hub = PrimeHub()
KP = 4

def drive_straight(distance_mm, speed=400):
    start = hub.imu.heading()                # LOCAL: created during the call
    error = hub.imu.heading() - start        # LOCAL: gone when the call ends
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
<h3>Local</h3>

- Made inside a function
- Gone the moment it returns
- `print(error)` outside → `NameError`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
<h3>Global</h3>

- Made at the top of the file
- Every function can **read** it
- Change it there once, and the whole robot is retuned
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The rescue slide for the hunt above; it moved here from *Name Your Moves* (decision #65) so the scope idea lands once, on the day the bug is felt, instead of being taught on D5 and re-hunted on D6. Show the `print(error)` → NameError live if the hunt didn't already. Then the D5 verbal pass, squad by squad: *default = factory setting · keyword = one-call override · top of file = global · inside a def = local*.
:::

# B. One Eye, One Edge {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

The robot **opens its eyes**, then parks one on a line's edge. 👁️

## Meet the eye 🔦

A **flashlight + light meter** in one brick. It measures its own echo.

```{.python}
from pybricks.pupdevices import ColorSensor
from pybricks.parameters import Color   # the colour names, for the beeper test

left_eye = ColorSensor(Port.D)    # yours
right_eye = ColorSensor(Port.A)   # yours -- only if you fitted a second eye

left_eye.reflection()   # 0-100: % of its OWN light echoing back
left_eye.color()        # a name: Color.RED... (optional colour extension)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
Anything that changes the **echo** changes the number: ✨ gloss · 💡 light · 📏 height.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The live demo beats the diagram: run a `print(left_eye.reflection())` loop, hold the robot, and let students slide surfaces under the eye, tilt it, lift it — the number dances. Establish the active-sensor idea: it brings its own LED, so it mostly ignores the room, but gloss, sensor height, and strong ambient light still shift the echo — which is exactly why every surface gets its own calibration (next slide). `reflection()` vs `color()`: today reflection does all the work; `color()` names colors and gets a cameo here — its real job is the optional notes extension. The eye lives on port **D** on the coach's robot — check yours. Following needs only **one** eye; `square_on_line` at the end of today is the job that wants a second, on the spare port **A**.
:::

## Break it: the threshold you guessed 🔥

::: {.qbox}
[Last week the tape split at **50** (white 88, black 10). Does 50 still work on the **mat**? The **floor**?]{.qtitle}
:::

🤖 **Robots out.** Print `reflection()` across **three surfaces**: tape · mat · floor. Log white and black for each.

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
A threshold is a fact about a **surface**: read white · read black · **split the middle.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Let each squad predict *before* measuring — commitments make the surprise land. The printed mat just arrived (decision #23), so this is also the real calibration-transfer checkpoint from the plan: the numbers they log here ARE the re-logged thresholds. Expected outcome: the mat's white and the tape-field's white read differently (print ink vs paper, matte tarp vs tape), the split point moves, and the habit lands — look first, then split what you actually see. The glossy-table failure (black reading 60, `< 50` calling the line "clear" and driving over it) is the venue-day version of the same lesson; it lives as an interactive sim in the 🏠 appendix since we don't have a glossy table in the room — mention it, don't show it. The takeaway is a habit, not a number: re-read and re-split, every surface.
:::

## Fix it: calibrate, then decide with `if / elif` 🎚️

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1-2|3|4|5-6"}
# Calibrate FIRST -- measure, never guess
THRESHOLD = 50                      # for THIS surface
while True:
    if left_eye.color() == Color.RED:
        hub.speaker.beep(frequency=880)     # high beep on red
    elif left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
        hub.speaker.beep(frequency=220)     # low beep on a line
    wait(50)
```

🤖 **Robots out.** Threshold from *your* mat numbers: low beep on lines, high beep on red.

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
`elif` adds a road: *otherwise, check this next.* New surface → **re-calibrate the threshold, never the code.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
D5 gave them `if/else` for the one fork inside `turn`; today's just-in-time concept is `elif` (more than two roads) + comparisons as booleans. Keep it concrete — a boolean is the answer to a yes/no question the robot asks the world (`color() == RED`, `reflection() < 50`). `elif` = "otherwise, check this next." Tie it straight back to the three-surface ritual: the threshold is data you recalibrate per surface; the `if/elif` structure never changes. The mat's printed staff lines make the beeper test real mission geography — they're the same lines we follow and square on later today. If a squad is flying, mention `else` for the catch-all case, but don't gate on it.
:::

```

</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var X0=45, X1=715, EDGE=380;
  function reflAt(cx){
    // smooth transition across the edge at x=380 (± 40px)
    var t=(cx-(EDGE-40))/80;               // 0 on white side, 1 on black side
    t=Math.max(0,Math.min(1,t));
    return Math.round(88 - t*(88-10));     // 88 on white → 10 on black
  }
  SIM.def('edMove', function(v){
    var cx=X0 + (parseInt(v,10)/100)*(X1-X0);
    SIM.el('edEye').setAttribute('cx',cx.toFixed(1));
    var r=reflAt(cx), err=r-50, m=SIM.el('edMsg');
    if(Math.abs(err)<=6){ m.style.color='#00AE8D'; m.innerHTML='reflection <b>'+r+'</b> → error <b>'+(err>=0?'+':'')+err+'</b> · riding the edge, go straight ✓ 🎯'; }
    else if(err>0){ m.style.color='#1C355E'; m.innerHTML='reflection <b>'+r+'</b> → error <b>+'+err+'</b> · out on white, steer toward the line'; }
    else { m.style.color='#625D9C'; m.innerHTML='reflection <b>'+r+'</b> → error <b>'+err+'</b> · buried in black, steer back out'; }
  });
})();
</script>
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
`error = reflection − 50`: **+ on white · − on black · 0 on the edge.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Watch reflection live on a real robot first, over white then over black — read the two numbers aloud, split them, that's the threshold (re-do on the actual mat; venue lighting shifts it). Then the widget: drag the eye and narrate the single signed number. The key mental model is *edge*-following, not *line*-centering — one eye rides the boundary, half on black. Positive error = drifted onto white, negative = drifted onto black. This is deliberately the same shape as the gyro's `error = target − heading`. Don't mention P yet; just establish that one eye yields one clean error.
:::

## Break it: only two answers 🔥

::: {.qbox}
[Two moves only: *hard left* or *hard right*. Predict the path.]{.qtitle}
:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|2|3-4|5-7"}
while True:
    if left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
        left.run(LINE_SPEED + TURN_HARD)       # on black → yank right
        right.run(LINE_SPEED - TURN_HARD)
    else:
        left.run(LINE_SPEED - TURN_HARD)       # on white → yank left
        right.run(LINE_SPEED + TURN_HARD)
    wait(10)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
Two answers means it can **never** go straight. It slams left-right forever.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is **bang-bang** — the naïve controller. Let them predict, then confirm with the sim two slides on. The diagnosis you want in their words: "it only knows left or right, so it's always turning." The bridge to P is exactly the KP quiz from Day 4: what if the correction were *proportional* to how far off we are, instead of always full-tilt? Keep bang-bang short — it exists only to make P feel like the rescue.
:::

## Name it: P, proportional steering 📈

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|2-3"}
error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD    # signed: how far off the edge?
left.run(LINE_SPEED + KP * error)            # far → hard steer,
right.run(LINE_SPEED - KP * error)           # near → gentle
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
`error × KP` **again**. Tune **`KP`**: too small = lazy, too big = the wobble is back.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The "aha" is that they've written this line before — twice. It's *literally* the D4 self-healing straight with a new error source: swap `hub.imu.heading()` for the eye's reflection and the two `run` lines are identical. Same `error × KP`, different sensor feeding it. Two failure modes to name so they recognize them on the bench: sluggish (KP too low) drifts wide on curves; twitchy (KP too high) reintroduces the wobble. Start small and adjust. This alone wins "Line King" on gentle lines — but push the speed up on a curve and it starts to overshoot, which is the doorway to the PD stretch. If a student raises the "use `motor.dc()`" advice here: same answer as the D4 proportional-turn coach note — `run()` keeps "speed" meaning speed, so `KP * error` stays a correction in deg/s they can reason about.
:::

# C. P → PD, and Squaring {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #625D9C)"}

Push P fast into a curve and an old ghost comes back. 🛑

## Feel it: race all three 🎢

::: {.qbox}
[Run **P** *fast* into a curve and predict the moment it lets go.]{.qtitle}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="sim">
  <div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:10px;margin-bottom:6px;flex-wrap:wrap;">
    <button class="sim-btn ghost small" id="lfBB" data-sim="lfMode" data-sim-arg="bb">bang-bang</button>
    <button class="sim-btn ghost small" id="lfP" data-sim="lfMode" data-sim-arg="p">P</button>
    <button class="sim-btn teal small" id="lfPD" data-sim="lfMode" data-sim-arg="pd">PD</button>
    <button class="sim-btn small" data-sim="lfGo">▶ run</button>
  </div>
  <div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:22px;font-size:15px;color:#1C355E;font-weight:700;margin-bottom:4px;">
    <span>speed <input type="range" min="80" max="320" step="10" value="200" data-sim-input="lfSet" data-sim-arg="v" style="width:120px;accent-color:#1C355E;"> <span id="lfVv">200</span></span>
    <span>KP <input type="range" min="0.2" max="3" step="0.1" value="1.2" data-sim-input="lfSet" data-sim-arg="kp" style="width:120px;accent-color:#00AE8D;"> <span id="lfKpv">1.2</span></span>
    <span>KD <input type="range" min="0" max="8" step="0.2" value="4" data-sim-input="lfSet" data-sim-arg="kd" style="width:120px;accent-color:#E96852;"> <span id="lfKdv">4.0</span></span>
  </div>
  <svg width="880" height="178" viewBox="0 0 880 240" style="display:block;margin:0 auto;background:#f2f5f9;border-radius:14px;">
    <path id="lfLine" d="" fill="none" stroke="#101820" stroke-width="10" stroke-linecap="round"/>
    <polyline id="lfPath" points="" fill="none" stroke="#00C9A7" stroke-width="3"/>
    <g id="lfBot" transform="translate(40,120) rotate(90)"><g transform="scale(0.5)">
      <use href="#sim-bot-mini"/>
    </g></g>
    <text id="lfTag" x="440" y="28" font-size="17" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#625D9C">PD: reads far AND fast</text>
  </svg>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var raf=null, last=null, mode='pd', V=200, KP=1.2, KD=4.0;
  var X0=40, X1=840, midY=120, G=0.6;
  // the line the bot must follow: straight lead-in, then an S-curve
  function edgeY(x){
    if(x<300) return midY;
    return midY + 70*Math.sin((x-300)/90);
  }
  function drawLine(){
    var d='M '+X0+' '+edgeY(X0).toFixed(1);
    for(var x=X0+6;x<=X1;x+=6) d+=' L '+x.toFixed(1)+' '+edgeY(x).toFixed(1);
    SIM.el('lfLine').setAttribute('d',d);
  }
  var TAGS={bb:['bang-bang: only two answers','#E96852'],p:['P: reads how FAR off','#00AE8D'],pd:['PD: reads far AND fast','#625D9C']};
  function setBtns(){
    [['bb','lfBB'],['p','lfP'],['pd','lfPD']].forEach(function(pair){
      var on=mode===pair[0], b=SIM.el(pair[1]);
      b.style.background=on?'#00C9A7':'#eef3f8'; b.style.color=on?'#fff':'#1C355E'; b.style.border=on?'none':'2px solid #1C355E';
    });
    SIM.el('lfTag').textContent=TAGS[mode][0]; SIM.el('lfTag').setAttribute('fill',TAGS[mode][1]);
  }
  SIM.def('lfMode', function(m){ mode=m; setBtns(); });
  SIM.def('lfSet', function(k,v){
    if(k==='v'){ V=parseInt(v,10); SIM.el('lfVv').textContent=v; }
    if(k==='kp'){ KP=parseFloat(v); SIM.el('lfKpv').textContent=parseFloat(v).toFixed(1); }
    if(k==='kd'){ KD=parseFloat(v); SIM.el('lfKdv').textContent=parseFloat(v).toFixed(1); }
  });
  SIM.def('lfGo', function(){
    var x=X0, y=edgeY(X0), th=0, lastErr=0, wApplied=0, pts=[]; last=null;
    SIM.el('lfPath').setAttribute('points','');
    function frame(now){
      var dt=last?Math.min((now-last)/1000,0.04):0.016; last=now;
      var sd=0.006, n=Math.max(1,Math.round(dt/sd));
      for(var i=0;i<n && x<X1;i++){
        var e=(edgeY(x)-y)*G;                 // + when bot is above the line (on white)
        if(e>50)e=50; if(e<-50)e=-50;
        var wDesired;
        if(mode==='bb'){ wDesired=(e>0?1:-1)*3.2; }
        else if(mode==='p'){ wDesired=KP*e*0.09; }
        else { wDesired=KP*e*0.09 + KD*(e-lastErr)*0.09; }
        lastErr=e;
        wApplied += (wDesired-wApplied)*0.30;  // steering/motor lag -- a real robot can't flip direction instantly
        th += wApplied*sd*6;
        if(th>1.2)th=1.2; if(th<-1.2)th=-1.2;
        y += V*Math.tan(th)*sd;
        x += V*sd;
        if(y<20)y=20; if(y>220)y=220;
      }
      pts.push(x.toFixed(1)+','+y.toFixed(1));
      SIM.el('lfPath').setAttribute('points',pts.join(' '));
      SIM.el('lfPath').setAttribute('stroke', mode==='bb'?'#E96852':(mode==='p'?'#00AE8D':'#00C9A7'));
      SIM.el('lfBot').setAttribute('transform','translate('+x.toFixed(1)+','+y.toFixed(1)+') rotate('+(90+th*57.3).toFixed(1)+')');
      if(x<X1){ raf=requestAnimationFrame(frame); } else raf=null;
    }
    if(raf)cancelAnimationFrame(raf); drawLine(); raf=requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  });
  drawLine(); setBtns();
})();
</script>
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .purple}
**bang-bang** ping-pongs · **P** overshoots · **PD** holds. Drag **KD → 0**: **D is the only difference.**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Run bang-bang first (big zigzag), then P at speed 200 (fine on the straight, overshoots into the S), then PD (clean). The money move is live: with PD selected, drag KD to 0 — the green curve starts ringing exactly like P; nudge it back up and it settles. That's the same demonstration as Day 5's kd slider on the gyro, now on the line — same D, same job, new sensor. Crank the speed slider to show P's overshoot grows with speed while PD holds. Sim is illustrative; on the real robot they tune KP first, and only squads chasing the stretch touch kd.
:::

## Name it: `follow_line` joins the library 📦 {.code-shrink}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|3|4|5-6|7|8-9|12"}
def follow_line(distance_mm, speed=250, kd=0):
    """P follow on the LEFT eye. kd > 0 is the PD stretch."""
    finish = left.angle() + distance_mm * DEG_PER_MM
    last_error = 0
    while left.angle() < finish:
        error = left_eye.reflection() - THRESHOLD
        steer = KP_LINE * error + kd * (error - last_error)
        left.run(speed + steer)
        right.run(speed - steer)
        last_error = error
        wait(10)
    left.stop(); right.stop()
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
The P loop, **bottled**. A finish line in degrees makes it a *segment*, and **`kd`** is the stretch knob.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Same promotion ritual as every day this week: the loose P loop gets a name and moves into `movements.py` (its `KP` becomes `KP_LINE` — the library's constants block already owns `KP` for the gyro). Map every part back to what they own: `error` = P on the eye, the `finish` line = `drive_straight`'s DEG_PER_MM trick (follow *for a distance* — that's how missions call it), `kd * (error - last_error)` = the D from the library-day gyro turn, with `last_error` the one-line memory that makes D possible. The gate is the P version — `follow_line(600)` with kd=0; the stretch is sliding kd up until the fast curve stops overshooting, which is what wins Speed Demon. State the I-policy plainly and move on: integral fixes a *steady* offset over a *long* run; our segments are short, so I is a demo they can watch but never something the gate depends on.
:::

## Two eyes, one question: `not`, `and`, `or` 🧠 {.smaller}

::: {.qbox}
[Each wheel parks when **its own** eye hits the line. The loop must run until **both** have parked. What goes at the top of the `while`?]{.qtitle}
:::

| Check | True when… |
|:--|:--|
| `not left_done` | the left wheel is **still driving** |
| `left_done and right_done` | **both** wheels have parked |
| `left_done or right_done` | **at least one** has parked |

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
| `left_done` | `right_done` | `left_done and right_done` | the loop |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:--|
| False | False | False | keeps going |
| True | False | False | keeps going |
| False | True | False | keeps going |
| True | True | **True** | **leaves** |

::: {.cardbox .teal}
`while not (left_done and right_done):` keep going while it is **not** true that both are done.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The course's one lesson on `not` / `and` / `or` (decision #65), placed on the first verb that genuinely needs two conditions. Predict each row aloud before the fragment. The argument worth having: someone will propose `while not left_done or not right_done:`. It is also correct; say so, and say the `not (… and …)` version reads closer to the English. `or` is not used in this verb, but it is on the card on purpose: *Stop at the Wall*'s `wall_square` reuses this exact `and`, and the claw lesson's checking loop ends when the jaw is stalled **or** done.
:::

## The two-eye job: square up 📐 {.code-shrink}

The **second** eye's moment: you hit a junction **crooked**, so sit square before the next move.

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|3|4|5|6-7|8-9|10"}
def square_on_line(speed=160):
    """Stop each wheel as ITS OWN eye reaches the line."""
    left_done = right_done = False
    left.run(speed); right.run(speed)
    while not (left_done and right_done):
        if not left_done and left_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            left.hold(); left_done = True      # park left wheel
        if not right_done and right_eye.reflection() < THRESHOLD:
            right.hold(); right_done = True    # park right wheel
        wait(5)
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .purple}
Each eye stops **its own** wheel, so the robot **pivots square**. *That's* why it carries two.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .coral}
👁️ **One eye can't do this, and it's worth knowing why.** One reading tells you that you **are** on the line. It never tells you whether you're **crooked** on it: a robot 20° askew and a robot dead square give the same number.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
So a one-eye robot squares on a **wall** instead. Both wheels press the same flat edge, and the edge does the aligning. Two eyes square on a **line**, anywhere on the mat. That's the trade the spare port buys.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Answer the port question head-on, and answer it with **our** robot, not the kit: the eye is on **D**, the two grippers take **E** and **C**, the drive motors **F** and **B** — which leaves exactly **one** spare port, **A**. Following needs one eye; this verb wants two. So the second eye is a *purchase*, and A is the money. Say what it costs: spend A on an eye and you can never add a third mechanism — though the 4-motor cap (§5.2.8) was going to stop you anyway. On the real mat this kills accumulated drift in a fraction of a second, gold going into the later integrated runs. (The same second eye later reads note colours in the optional extension — but never steers.)
:::

## Watch it snap square 📐

```{=html}
<div class="sim">
  <div class="sim-controls">
    <button class="sim-btn purple" data-sim="sqGo">▶ creep onto the junction</button>
  </div>
  <svg width="420" height="272" viewBox="0 0 420 272" style="display:block;margin:0 auto;background:#f2f5f9;border-radius:14px;">
    <rect x="0" y="60" width="420" height="14" fill="#101820"/>
    <text x="380" y="52" font-size="13" fill="#625D9C" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle">junction</text>
    <g id="sqBot" transform="translate(210,178) rotate(-16)">
      <rect x="-26" y="-30" width="52" height="70" rx="8" fill="#1C355E"/>
      <circle id="sqLE" cx="-16" cy="-30" r="6" fill="#FFD500" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2"/>
      <circle id="sqRE" cx="16" cy="-30" r="6" fill="#FFD500" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2"/>
    </g>
    <text id="sqMsg" x="210" y="262" font-size="16" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1C355E">arrives crooked: each eye stops its own wheel</text>
  </svg>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var raf=null, last=null, LINEY=67;
  SIM.def('sqGo', function(){
    var cx=210, cy=178, th=-0.28;            // start below, skewed
    var phase='drive', px=0, py=0, sgn=1; last=null;
    SIM.el('sqMsg').setAttribute('fill','#1C355E'); SIM.el('sqMsg').textContent='creeping up, skewed…';
    // eye local coords: left (-16,-30), right (16,-30) → world
    function eyeWorld(lx,ly){ return {x: cx+lx*Math.cos(th)-ly*Math.sin(th), y: cy+lx*Math.sin(th)+ly*Math.cos(th)}; }
    function frame(now){
      var dt=last?Math.min((now-last)/1000,0.04):0.016; last=now;
      if(phase==='drive'){
        cy -= 70*Math.cos(th)*dt; cx += 70*Math.sin(th)*dt;   // both wheels rolling
        var le=eyeWorld(-16,-30), re=eyeWorld(16,-30);
        if(le.y<=LINEY || re.y<=LINEY){                       // leading eye reaches the line
          var leftLeads = le.y<=LINEY;
          px=(leftLeads?le:re).x; py=LINEY;                   // that wheel parks, pivot here
          sgn = th<0 ? 1 : -1;                                // trailing wheel swings body square
          phase='pivot';
          SIM.el('sqMsg').textContent=(leftLeads?'left':'right')+' eye on the line: its wheel parks, the other creeps on';
        }
      } else if(phase==='pivot'){
        var dth=sgn*0.9*dt;
        if((sgn>0 && th+dth>=0) || (sgn<0 && th+dth<=0)){ dth=-th; phase='done'; }
        var ox=cx-px, oy=cy-py, c=Math.cos(dth), s=Math.sin(dth);
        cx=px+ox*c-oy*s; cy=py+ox*s+oy*c; th+=dth;            // rotate body about the parked eye
      }
      SIM.el('sqBot').setAttribute('transform','translate('+cx.toFixed(1)+','+cy.toFixed(1)+') rotate('+(th*57.3).toFixed(1)+')');
      if(phase==='done'){
        raf=null; SIM.el('sqMsg').setAttribute('fill','#00AE8D');
        SIM.el('sqMsg').textContent='squared ✓ · heading reset to 0°, position error gone';
        return;
      }
      raf=requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }
    if(raf)cancelAnimationFrame(raf); raf=requestAnimationFrame(frame);
  });
})();
</script>
```

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.cardbox .purple}
Leading wheel parks first · trailing wheel swings square · **drift gone.** 🎯
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Run it live: the bot arrives crooked, one wheel stops on the line first, the other pivots the body until its eye lands too — square. This is exactly `square_on_line()` from the previous slide. On the mat it erases accumulated drift in a fraction of a second, right before the next move — cheap, automatic insurance the later integrated runs lean on.
:::

# D. Compete & Gate {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Today's showdown: **Line King** 👑, and for the fast squads, **Speed Demon.** 🏁

## Line King 👑 / Speed Demon 🏁

::: {.callout-important}
## The challenge
**Line King:** hold the curved line for **30 s**, on accuracy and speed.
**Speed Demon** *(fast squads)*: the fastest run that **never leaves the line.**
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The winning recipe**

- Calibrate **on the mat you run on**
- Tune **`KP_LINE`**, *then* chase speed
- **Square** at the junction to reset
- *(stretch)* **`kd`** kills the curve overshoot
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where squads lose it**

- Threshold from *last week's tape*, not this mat 😬
- `KP` so high the straight wobbles
- Skipping the square → drift compounds
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Line King rewards a clean, honest tune over raw speed; Speed Demon is the stretch for squads whose P was solid early and who took the kd upgrade. Coach's eye is on the *tuning conversation*, not the trophy: can they explain what the error means, what KP_LINE did, and why the threshold had to be re-measured on this mat? That explanation IS the gate (kd talk is stretch credit, not a requirement). Keep the taped junction handy so squaring gets used under pressure, not just demoed.
:::

## Today's gate

::: {.callout-important}
## You're done today when…
- You can **build, tune, and explain** a P line-follower
- It **follows a curve** reliably
- **Two eyes:** it **squares on a junction** with `square_on_line`
- **One eye:** you can *show* why it can't, because crooked and square read the same, and the job carries to tomorrow's wall
- **`follow_line`** lives in your `movements.py` *(it gains `kd=` for the PD stretch)*
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Next: *Stop at the Wall*. The motor becomes a **sensor**, and the wall **resets the truth**. 🧱
:::

::: {.notes}
The gate is the plan's line-day outcome: build, tune, and *explain* a P follower + reliable junction squaring — what the anchor run actually uses. Split the squaring half by build, because our competition robot runs **one** eye and `square_on_line` genuinely needs two: a two-eye squad demonstrates the verb, a one-eye squad demonstrates the *failure* (park it crooked on the line, read the number, park it square, read the same number) and carries the job to tomorrow, where `wall_square` solves it on the border. Do not fail a one-eye squad for a sensor it was never given. The `heading=` argument is tomorrow's idea too — declaring a heading is D7's "the wall never lies", so name it, don't teach it today; PD is explicitly the stretch, never the gate. A student who can narrate why each term is there owns the concept and can debug it during integration when the follower serves the run. Two eyes, one job each: one follows, both square. Close by pointing forward: tomorrow the motor itself becomes a sensor — the robot feels walls, patrols between them, and resets its heading truth against them — and the scoresheet gets read the anchor-first way: everything those color-free verbs score comes first.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="sim">
  <div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:14px;margin-bottom:8px;">
    <span style="font-size:16px;color:#1C355E;font-weight:700;">surface:</span>

    <input id="rmTh" type="range" min="0" max="100" step="1" value="50" data-sim-input="rmTh" style="width:170px;accent-color:#E96852;">

    <defs><linearGradient id="rmGrad" x1="0" x2="1"><stop offset="0" stop-color="#101820"/><stop offset="1" stop-color="#ffffff"/></linearGradient></defs>
    <text x="60" y="105" font-size="14" fill="#1C355E" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">0 · dark</text>
    <text x="760" y="105" font-size="14" fill="#1C355E" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">100 · bright</text>
    <!-- threshold line -->
    <line id="rmThLine" x1="410" y1="44" x2="410" y2="98" stroke="#E96852" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>
    <text id="rmThTxt" x="410" y="38" font-size="13" fill="#E96852" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle">50</text>
    <!-- markers -->
    <g id="rmBlack"><circle cy="71" r="11" fill="#1C355E" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2"/><text y="132" font-size="13" fill="#1C355E" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle">black line</text></g>
    <g id="rmWhite"><circle cy="71" r="11" fill="#FFD500" stroke="#1C355E" stroke-width="2"/><text y="132" font-size="13" fill="#1C355E" font-weight="800" text-anchor="middle">white mat</text></g>
  </svg>
  <div id="rmVerdict" style="text-align:center;font-family:Consolas,monospace;font-size:19px;color:#1C355E;font-weight:700;min-height:28px;">pick a surface and read what the eye actually sees</div>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  var X0=60, X1=760, thr=50, surf=null;
  var S={ home:{white:88, black:10}, gloss:{white:95, black:60} };
  function xOf(v){ return X0 + v/100*(X1-X0); }
  function draw(){
    SIM.el('rmThLine').setAttribute('x1',xOf(thr)); SIM.el('rmThLine').setAttribute('x2',xOf(thr));
    SIM.el('rmThTxt').setAttribute('x',xOf(thr)); SIM.el('rmThTxt').textContent=thr;
    if(!surf) return;
    var s=S[surf];
    SIM.el('rmBlack').setAttribute('transform','translate('+xOf(s.black).toFixed(1)+',0)');
    SIM.el('rmWhite').setAttribute('transform','translate('+xOf(s.white).toFixed(1)+',0)');
    var blackOK = s.black < thr;   // robot must call the dark line "line"
    var whiteOK = s.white > thr;   // and the bright mat "clear"
    var v=SIM.el('rmVerdict');
    if(blackOK && whiteOK){
      v.style.color='#00AE8D';
      v.innerHTML='black '+s.black+' &lt; '+thr+' → <b>LINE ✓</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; white '+s.white+' &gt; '+thr+' → <b>clear ✓</b> &nbsp; 🎯';
    } else {
      v.style.color='#E96852';
      var msg = !blackOK ? ('black reads '+s.black+', <b>above '+thr+'</b>, so the robot calls the line "clear" and drives right over it. 😬')
                         : ('white reads '+s.white+', <b>below '+thr+'</b>, so the robot brakes on empty mat. 😬');
      v.innerHTML=msg;
    }
  }
  SIM.def('rmSurf', function(k){
    surf=k;
    SIM.el('rmHome').style.background = k==='home' ? '#00C9A7':'#eef3f8';
    SIM.el('rmHome').style.color = k==='home' ? '#fff':'#1C355E';
    SIM.el('rmHome').style.border = k==='home' ? 'none':'2px solid #1C355E';
    SIM.el('rmGloss').style.background = k==='gloss' ? '#00C9A7':'#eef3f8';
    SIM.el('rmGloss').style.color = k==='gloss' ? '#fff':'#1C355E';
    SIM.el('rmGloss').style.border = k==='gloss' ? 'none':'2px solid #1C355E';
    draw();
  });
  SIM.def('rmTh', function(v){ thr=parseInt(v,10); SIM.el('rmThV').textContent=v; draw(); });
  SIM.run('rmSurf', 'home');
})();
</script>
```

On a glossy venue table, "black" can bounce back **60**. Drag the threshold and rescue the robot.
